purpose: Sorts the open findings of a run into three lists: changes that can go in now, changes that need planning, and changes that can lock a person or a mailbox out, naming the accounts the run's own data shows would be affected. Read by Get-TPChangeImpact.
rules: Implement now: licensed, and the control's operational-impact archetype is one of Get-TPLowFrictionArchetypes (documented as invisible to users), and the control is not listed under accountRisk.
Could break accounts: every control listed under accountRisk, and every open control whose operational impact is not documented (an undocumented impact is not evidence of no impact).
Needs planning: every other licensed open control.
A control the tenant is not confirmed licensed for is listed under license decisions, never in the three lists.

Accounts are named only from data the run read. A source that was not read, failed, or stopped at a page cap says so; 'none found' is said only after a complete read, and never means nothing can break.

evidenceTypes.LegacyAuthSignIns: Successful sign-ins through a legacy authentication client in the sign-in log window (AAD-SignInEvidence, LegacyAuth). These accounts stop signing in through that client once it is blocked.
evidenceTypes.SingleFactorSignIns: Successful interactive sign-ins whose recorded authentication steps show no second factor (AAD-SignInEvidence, SingleFactor). These accounts are prompted for MFA once it is required.
evidenceTypes.MfaUnregistered: Enabled accounts with no MFA method registered (AAD-Users, MFARegistration). They must register at their next sign-in; an account that cannot (a shared or service account signing in interactively) is blocked.
evidenceTypes.AdminsWithoutPhishResistant: Accounts holding an admin role with no phishing-resistant method registered (FIDO2 security key, device-bound passkey, Windows Hello for Business, macOS platform credential). They cannot complete an admin sign-in once phishing-resistant MFA is required.
evidenceTypes.PhoneOnlyMfa: Accounts whose only MFA methods are phone methods (text or voice). They lose their second factor when SMS and voice are disabled.
evidenceTypes.PrivilegedPermanent: Permanent (active, not PIM-eligible) privileged role assignments (AAD-DirectoryRoles). These holders lose standing access when assignments move to PIM eligibility.
evidenceTypes.GlobalAdmins: Global Administrator holders, permanent and eligible (AAD-DirectoryRoles). Bringing the count into range removes some of them.
evidenceTypes.PrivilegedHolders: Privileged role holders, permanent and eligible (AAD-DirectoryRoles). A device or workstation restriction for administrators applies to each of them.
evidenceTypes.SmtpAuthMailboxes: Mailboxes whose own setting enables SMTP AUTH (EXO-Inventory). Devices and applications that send through them with SMTP AUTH stop sending.
evidenceTypes.ForwardingMailboxes: Mailboxes forwarding to an external address (EXO-Inventory). Their forwarding stops.
evidenceTypes.ForwardingRules: Inbox rules forwarding or redirecting to an external address (EXO-Inventory). Those rules stop delivering outside the organization.
evidenceTypes.SharedMailboxSignIn: Shared mailboxes whose account can sign in directly (EXO-Inventory). Anyone signing in to them directly is blocked.
evidenceTypes.NonCompliantDevices: Users of Intune-managed devices that are not compliant (Intune-DeviceCompliance). They lose access from those devices when compliance is required; unenrolled devices are not seen by the tool at all.
evidenceTypes.EmergencyAccess: The tenant's approved emergency-access accounts (Config/baseline-exceptions/<tenant>.psd1). Not accounts that break: accounts every new policy must exclude so a mistake cannot lock the tenant out.

AAD-1.1.Why: Blocking legacy authentication stops every client that signs in with a password over an old protocol: older Outlook versions, phone mail apps using IMAP or ActiveSync with basic auth, scanners and scripts.

AAD-11.1.Why: Blocking the device code flow stops sign-ins on devices that use it: conference-room and shared devices, some command-line tools, and Teams Rooms on older builds.
AAD-11.1.Unseen: Device-code sign-ins are not read from the sign-in log (the authentication protocol cannot be filtered on the server), so the accounts that use the flow are not named. Check the sign-in log for authentication protocol 'Device code' before turning the block on.

AAD-1.2.Why: Requiring MFA for everyone blocks any account that cannot complete it: accounts with no method registered that cannot register (shared or service accounts signing in interactively), and anything signing in without a second factor today.

AAD-1.3.Why: Requiring phishing-resistant MFA for administrators blocks every admin sign-in from an account without a FIDO2 key, passkey, Windows Hello for Business or platform credential.

AAD-1.4.Why: A sign-in risk policy that requires MFA blocks a risky sign-in by an account that has no MFA method to answer with.

AAD-1.5.Why: A user risk policy that requires a secure password change blocks a risky account that cannot complete MFA and self-service password reset.

AAD-2.1.Why: Turning on the core Conditional Access policies applies MFA and the legacy block to everyone at once; a policy without its emergency-access exclusion can lock out every administrator.

AAD-2.3.Why: Requiring a compliant device blocks sign-ins from every personal, unenrolled or non-compliant device.
AAD-2.3.Unseen: Unmanaged and unenrolled devices are invisible to the tool; their users are blocked too and are not named here.

INT-1.2.Why: Blocking non-compliant devices through Conditional Access stops access from every device Intune marks non-compliant, and from unenrolled devices.
INT-1.2.Unseen: Unmanaged and unenrolled devices are invisible to the tool; their users are blocked too and are not named here.

AAD-11.4.Why: Token protection rejects sessions from clients and platforms that cannot bind their token; users on those clients are signed out and cannot sign back in.
AAD-11.4.Unseen: Which clients each user signs in from is not read. Start the policy in report-only and read its results before enforcing it.

AAD-11.5.Why: Strict location enforcement ends sessions when the IP address seen by the resource differs from the one seen at sign-in, which breaks users behind split-tunnel VPNs and some proxies.
AAD-11.5.Unseen: Network paths are not read. Start in report-only and read the results before enforcing it.

AAD-11.7.Why: Restricting administrators to privileged access workstations or compliant devices blocks every admin sign-in from any other device.

AAD-17.3.Why: Disabling SMS and voice removes the only second factor of every account that registered nothing else; they cannot complete MFA until they register another method.

AAD-3.1.Why: Bringing the Global Administrator count into range removes the role from some accounts; whoever relied on it loses that access, and the emergency-access accounts must keep it.

AAD-3.2.Why: Moving permanent admin assignments to PIM eligibility removes standing access: each holder must activate the role before using it. Emergency-access accounts must stay permanent.

EXO-1.2.Why: Disabling SMTP AUTH for the organization stops every device and application that sends mail by signing in to Exchange Online over SMTP: scanners, line-of-business apps, older printers.

EXO-1.6.Why: Requiring modern authentication for Exchange Online stops every mail client still signing in with basic authentication.

EXO-2.3.Why: Disabling POP3 stops every mail client and device that collects mail over POP3.
EXO-2.3.Unseen: POP3 clients that use modern authentication are not in the legacy sign-in read.

EXO-2.4.Why: Disabling IMAP stops every mail client and device that reads mail over IMAP.
EXO-2.4.Unseen: IMAP clients that use modern authentication are not in the legacy sign-in read.

EXO-7.4.Why: Removing per-mailbox SMTP AUTH overrides stops the devices and applications sending through those mailboxes.

SPO-1.3.Why: Blocking legacy authentication to SharePoint stops old Office clients and tools that sign in to SharePoint with a password.

EXO-1.3.Why: Blocking external auto-forwarding stops every mailbox forwarding and inbox rule that sends mail outside the organization.

EXO-7.1.Why: Removing external mailbox forwarding stops mail reaching wherever those mailboxes forward it.

EXO-7.2.Why: Removing external forwarding rules stops mail reaching wherever those rules send it.

EXO-2.6.Why: Blocking sign-in on shared mailboxes stops anyone who signs in to one directly instead of opening it from their own account.
